details:
Earth Jukebox: Hearing a Changing Planet

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Challenge: The Earth Information Jukebox · Project

NOVALITHA

Team: NOVALITHA · Members: Anna Rose, Binitta Rose, Cleetus T J, Mebin Babu, Niya Maria

1. Summary

Earth Jukebox is a single-file, browser-based instrument that turns Earth-observation image

frames into live sound. A playhead sweeps across a frame from west to east. Each band of

latitude becomes a musical note, and the strength of the signal in that band sets how loud it is.

Colour changes the instrument, and the amount of fine detail changes the rhythm. Because the

sound is generated in real time from the pixels, any frame a person loads can be heard.

We built it so that people who cannot see a map, or who find dense maps hard to read, can still

follow what a satellite sees. We also built it so that anyone can hear change: step through

consecutive days and listen to haze spread, thin and move.

2. The challenge

The challenge asks for an "Earth Jukebox": an interface, script or application that pairs Earth

Information Center (EIC) visual frames with dynamic sonifications generated in real time, so

that complex Earth science becomes accessible, engaging and multi-sensory. It encourages

computer-vision-style analysis of colour, shape and pixel density, mapped to pitch, tempo and

instrumentation. It asks teams to balance data translation with musicality, to treat accessibility

as a core theme, and to tell the story behind the choices.

3. What we built

A self-contained web page (one HTML file, about 220 KB, no external libraries, works offline)

that:

• Opens with three real NASA satellite frames already loaded, so a judge can press Play

immediately.

• Offers six sound styles, Side A to Side F. They use the same satellite frames and change

only the scale and tone.

• Lets anyone load their own frames (one or several) and plays them as a time sequence.

• Records the result as a downloadable audio file.

4. Data used

Item Detail

Imagery Three true-colour satellite frames

over South Asia from consecutive

Item Detail days Dates Day 1: 11 Nov 2026. Day 2: 12 Nov 2026. Day 3: [confirm the date] Layer / instrument Terra / MODIS, Corrected Reflectance (True Color); layer name MODIS_Terra_CorrectedReflectance_T rueColor Source NASA Worldview (worldview.earthdata.nasa.gov) Preparation Each frame was cropped to a 2:1 strip (keeping the Himalayan foothills and the northern plains), resized and compressed as JPEG, then embedded in the page The frames show winter-season haze lying over the northern plains, snow and cloud over the Himalaya and Tibetan Plateau, cloud over the Bay of Bengal, and black wedges where the satellite did not cover the ground. Seasonal haze in this region is a recurring public-health concern, which made it a meaningful subject for a first demonstration. All data in the project is real NASA imagery. Nothing in it is synthetic. 5. How the sonification works Every frame is drawn onto a 360 × 180 grid. The sound engine then reads that grid as a moving window. Image property Sound property Why Position left to right Time (one pass takes 30 seconds at normal speed; speed is adjustable) Reading order matches how maps are read Position top to bottom, in 12 bands Pitch: higher in the frame is higher in pitch A natural "up is high" metaphor Brightness or signal strength in a band Loudness, and how bright the tone sounds (filter opening) Stronger signal is louder Dominant colour in a column Instrument: warm tones play a bright sawtooth, green a soft triangle, blue a pure sine Colour becomes timbre; low-colour areas keep the default voice Amount of fine detail in a column Pulse rate, from about 48 to 180 beats per minute Busy areas feel busy Image property Sound property Why Black (no data) Silence Missing data should not be mistaken for a quiet Earth To keep the result musical rather than chaotic, all twelve voices are tuned to a pentatonic or similar scale, so any combination of loud and quiet bands sounds consonant. A gentle low-pass filter and an echo smooth the output. The engine is built on the Web Audio API and generates every sound live; there are no pre-recorded clips. Sides A to F The six sides are sound styles applied to the same data: Side A (bright major pentatonic), Side B (high, glassy lydian bells), Side C (soft strings), Side D (low, dark minor), Side E (light, airy suspended tones) and Side F (deep dorian swells). They change how the data sounds, not what the data is. Two analysis modes • Haze mode (approximate). Instead of raw brightness, it scores each pixel with a colour rule that favours grey-beige, mid-brightness, low-saturation pixels, which is how thin haze looks in true colour, and plays that score. It also shows the score as a heat map so people can see what they are hearing. • Hear change between days. It subtracts one day from the next and plays the size of the difference. Louder means more change. It combines with haze mode to play change in the haze estimate. Time-lapse With time-lapse on, each sweep moves on to the next day, so one listen takes the audience through the whole sequence. A slider and the N and P keys step through frames manually. 6. Accessibility The challenge names accessibility as a core theme, so we treated it as part of the design, not an add-on: • The page works without sight: everything important is audible, and every frame has an automatically generated text description (which band is strongest and weakest, where the peak is, how detailed the frame is, and whether black gaps are present). • A Read description button speaks the description. Day changes are announced to screen readers, and spoken announcements are optional. • Full keyboard control: Space for play and pause, arrows to scrub, N and P for frames, H for haze mode, C for change, T for time-lapse, R to record, and ? for the shortcut list. • A high-contrast mode, a visible focus outline, larger touch targets on phones, and reduced-motion support. • Optional vibration on supported phones, pulsing with the rhythm, as a tactile channel. • A short "Start here" guide and an on-page legend for first-time visitors. 7. Telling the story Maps are silent. A person who is blind or has low vision, or a person who simply cannot read a dense colour map at a glance, is shut out of the picture that satellites provide. Sound can carry the same pattern: where the signal is strong, where it is weak, and how it shifts from one day to the next. We chose haze over South Asia as our demonstration because it is a changing system that people live inside. When the time-lapse plays, the listener hears the loudest regions drift and spread from day to day. We wanted the experience to carry some of the urgency of a changing planet without claiming more than the data supports, which is why the limits below are part of the project and not a footnote. 8. Limitations and honesty about the data • The sound follows brightness, not true measured values. In the default mode, bright clouds and snow are as loud as haze. The instrument shows where an image is bright or colourful, not how much pollution is present. • Haze mode is an estimate. It is a colour rule we designed, not a validated aerosol measurement. It is imperfect, and thin cloud or bright land can be mistaken for haze. • Change mode shows size, not direction. It does not say whether haze increased or cleared. • Resolution is low. Frames are reduced to a 360 × 180 grid, and the embedded samples are compressed, so fine features are lost. • The samples are cropped. The three frames were cut to a 2:1 strip, so the southern part of the peninsula is not included. • Regional frames are not a whole-world map. For regional images the page reports position as a percentage across and down the frame, not as latitude and longitude, to avoid false precision. • Missing data is silent. Black satellite-swath gaps are treated as no data, but they can look like quiet areas to a listener unless the description is read. For a research-grade version, the colour-to-value step should be replaced with real data values, such as an aerosol optical depth layer, instead of colour. 9. How to run it 1. Open the project link, or open earth-jukebox.html in a modern browser such as Chrome. No installation or internet connection is needed for the file. 2. Press Play. The three sample days load automatically. 3. Choose Side A to Side F to change the sound style. 4. Drag across the map to hear any single spot. 5. Try Haze mode and Hear change between days. 6. To use new imagery, choose one or more image files under Load EIC frame(s). Name multiple files in order, such as frame01.png, frame02.png. Use flat map views, and crop out legends and labels. 7. Press Record full sequence to save the soundtrack as a WAV file. 10. Future work • Use real data values (for example aerosol optical depth) and a sign-aware change mode that distinguishes increase from decrease. • Add more EIC layers, such as temperature, sea ice and chlorophyll, and a built-in picker. • Support global map frames and animated sequences directly, and sync stereo position to longitude. • Run listening sessions with blind and low-vision users to tune the mappings. • Offer a server version that generates audio files in bulk for a curated playlist. 11. Tools, credits and Super Intelligence (SI) disclosure • Imagery: NASA satellite imagery obtained through NASA Worldview (Terra / MODIS, Corrected Reflectance (True Color)). We thank the NASA Earth Information Center and the Space Apps organisers for the challenge. • Built with: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and the browser's Web Audio API. No third-party libraries. The demo video was recorded with Playwright and encoded with FFmpeg, and the frames were cropped with Pillow. • SI use: Claude (by Anthropic), a Super Intelligence tool, helped write the code, the on- page text, this document and the demo video script. The team directed the design and reviewed the results. • Where SI is acknowledged: the demo video carries a visible "SI-generated video" watermark and file metadata. The code has a comment, a meta tag and a visible notice. Soundtracks recorded from the page carry an SI acknowledgment in their file metadata. • Not SI-generated: the satellite imagery itself, which is NASA data.
